Learn · Chapter 11

Chapter 11: The Nervous System

Your nervous system detects changes, processes information and directs responses throughout your body.

How your nervous system works

Receptors detect changes inside and outside the body. Neurons carry nerve impulses, and neurotransmitters carry chemical messages across synapses. The brain and spinal cord process this information and help direct a response.

By the end of this chapter, I can:

  • I can explain how neurons receive, carry and pass along information.
  • I can trace a signal from a sensory receptor through the central nervous system to an effector.
  • I can explain resting potential, action potentials and communication across a synapse.
  • I can compare somatic and autonomic control, including sympathetic and parasympathetic responses.
  • I can identify major brain regions and connect their structures with their functions.

Work through the lessons, then complete the chapter checks. Use the diagrams and practice activities to review. Your saved responses and vocabulary work are in Process Collection.

Nervous communication

Your nervous system detects changes and directs a . Some responses are voluntary, such as reaching for a glass. Others, such as a change in heart rate, happen without a conscious decision.

Nervous and endocrine systems work together

Conditions inside and outside your body keep changing. Temperature may rise, water levels may fall, or your muscles may need to work harder. means maintaining relatively stable internal conditions despite these changes.

The nervous and endocrine systems work together. The nervous system uses electrochemical messages: electrical changes along neurons and chemical signals between cells. The endocrine system uses hormones, which travel in the bloodstream. This chapter focuses on the nervous system.

Follow this sequence: sensory input → integration → motor output. Sensory input carries information about a change. Integration means processing that information. Motor output carries instructions for a to an effector, such as a muscle or gland.

A first look at the two main divisions

The () is the brain and spinal cord. The () consists of nerves linking the CNS with the rest of the body. You will study their subdivisions later.

Two main types of cells

A is a nerve cell that receives and carries information to other cells. Glial cells support and nourish neurons. They also help remove wastes and protect against infection.

A neuron is one cell. A nerve contains many nerve fibres bundled together inside protective tissue. Think of a cable containing many individual fibres.

Follow the parts of one neuron

A typical has dendrites, a , an and axon terminals. The cell body, also called the soma, contains the nucleus and other organelles and carries out the cell’s life processes.

Dendrites are short, branching extensions that receive information and carry it toward the cell body. Their branches provide a large receiving surface. The cell body processes incoming information. The axon carries nerve impulses away from the cell body.

An axon may be much longer than a . Some extend over a metre, allowing a neuron to communicate with a distant cell.

At the , information passes to another neuron or an . This junction is a . The small gap between the cells is the synaptic cleft. Lesson 6 explains how a chemical message crosses it.

Myelin and Schwann cells

Many axons have a fatty insulating covering called the sheath. Schwann cells form myelin around axons in the PNS. The gaps between myelin segments are nodes of Ranvier.

Myelin speeds up nerve impulses. In a myelinated axon, the is regenerated at each node. This is , often described as “jumping” from node to node. The axon remains continuous underneath the myelin.

In an unmyelinated axon, each neighbouring section of membrane produces the next part of the impulse. In a myelinated axon, the impulse is regenerated at the nodes instead.

Feature Myelinated axon Unmyelinated axon
Insulation Has a myelin sheath Does not have a myelin sheath
Pattern of conduction Saltatory conduction between nodes Regeneration along neighbouring membrane regions
Relative conduction speed Faster in this comparison Slower in this comparison
Tissue connection Myelinated axons contribute to white matter See Lesson 9 for the composition of grey matter

Myelin-producing cells: Schwann cells make myelin in the . Oligodendrocytes make it in the .

Why myelin damage matters

In multiple sclerosis (MS), damage to disrupts nerve signals. Symptoms can include numbness, tingling, muscle spasms, and problems with balance or coordination. Other possible symptoms include blurred vision, weakness, fatigue and slurred speech.

Key connection: damaged myelin → disrupted nerve signals → changes in sensation or movement. The effects depend on which pathways are affected.

Sensory neurons, interneurons and motor neurons

Three types of work together. A , also called an afferent neuron, carries information from a sensory toward the . The receptor may detect touch, light, sound or another change.

An processes and relays information within the CNS. A , also called an efferent neuron, carries instructions from the CNS to an , such as a muscle or gland.

A cat darts onto the road. The driver’s eyes detect the . Sensory information reaches the CNS, where it is processed. Motor neurons then carry instructions to the muscles that press the brake.

Structure Role in the pathway
Sensory receptor Detects a stimulus
Sensory neuron Carries sensory information toward the CNS
Interneuron Processes and relays information within the CNS
Motor neuron Carries instructions toward the effector
Effector Produces the

Classifying neurons by shape

Multipolar, bipolar and unipolar describe a ’s shape and the branches extending from its . Sensory, interneuron and motor describe its job. Check whether a question asks about shape or function.

A reflex arc is a rapid circuit

A is a rapid, involuntary to a . Follow this withdrawal pathway: → → → → . The spinal cord processes the incoming signal and sends instructions to the muscle that pulls the body part away.

Remember: withdrawal can begin before you consciously feel the stimulus. Information still reaches the brain, but the spinal circuit does not wait for a conscious decision.

Not every reflex needs an interneuron. For each diagram, trace the receptor, sensory route into the , processing site, motor route out and effector.

What makes a nerve impulse electrochemical?

A nerve impulse is electrochemical. Charged particles called ions, including sodium (Na⁺) and potassium (K⁺), move across the membrane. Their movement changes the voltage across it.

Unlike current in a metal wire, a nerve impulse depends on ions moving across the membrane.

Study four stages: resting state, , and . Start with the resting neuron before following the changes during an impulse.

1. Resting state

Membrane potential is the voltage difference across a cell membrane. A resting is slightly negative inside compared with outside. A typical is −70 mV. The minus sign tells you how the inside compares with the outside.

“Resting” means the neuron is not producing an . Ions still move, and the cell still uses energy to maintain its conditions.

Ion concentrations, leakage and the sodium-potassium pump

There is more K⁺ inside the and more Na⁺ outside. At rest, K⁺ moves out through leak channels more easily than Na⁺ moves in. Large negatively charged molecules remain inside the cell.

The sodium-potassium pump uses ATP to move 3 Na⁺ out for every 2 K⁺ moved in. This maintains the concentration differences across the membrane.

Channels and pumps do different jobs. Leakage through channels is passive. The pump uses ATP for active transport. Together, ion concentrations and the membrane’s help maintain the resting potential.

2. Depolarization and threshold

means the inside becomes less negative. In our example, the voltage rises from −70 mV toward the of about −55 mV.

Below threshold, a does not trigger an . At threshold, voltage-gated sodium channels open. Na⁺ enters the , making the inside more positive. In this example, the peak is about +40 mV.

Graphs may use a peak near +35 mV or +40 mV. These are example values, so read the values on the graph you are given.

3. Repolarization and hyperpolarization

After the peaks, sodium channels become inactivated and K⁺ moves out through potassium channels. Positive charge leaves, making the inside negative again. This is .

Potassium channels close slowly, so K⁺ may keep leaving briefly. The voltage drops below the resting level. This is , or the undershoot. The example here reaches about −90 mV before recovering.

The sodium-potassium pump maintains the ion concentration differences over time. Ion movement through channels causes the rapid rise and fall of an action potential.

Voltage is not concentration. The membrane voltage changes during an impulse, but the overall Na⁺ and K⁺ concentration gradients do not reverse.

4. The refractory period

The is a brief recovery time. At first, that part of the membrane cannot fire again. Later, it can fire only if the stimulus is stronger than usual.

This helps the impulse travel forward, called . The next section of the reaches while the section behind is recovering. The signal continues toward the axon terminals.

More detail: two parts of the refractory period
Two parts of recovery. During the a second cannot occur at that membrane region. During the , a stronger can trigger one. Recovery is not simply an on/off event at −70 mV.

All-or-none and stimulus strength

An is all-or-none: a fires when it reaches , or it does not. A stronger does not make that neuron’s individual action potential taller.

A stronger stimulus can produce more impulses per second and activate more neurons. These are different changes: faster firing versus more neurons firing. Neither makes each action potential larger.

How the impulse travels along the axon

An starts a new action potential in the next section of membrane. This produces a wave along the axon. In myelinated axons, the signal is regenerated at each .

allows the signal to spread quickly between nodes. The “jump” in describes where action potentials are regenerated. Sodium ions do not travel the full length of the .

Crossing a synapse

An travels along the to the . At a chemical , it cannot jump across the gap to the next . Instead, the sending neuron releases a chemical messenger called a .

Presynaptic means the sending side; postsynaptic means the receiving side. A synapse between a and a muscle cell is a neuromuscular junction.

Release, movement and binding

An reaches the . Calcium channels open, and Ca²⁺ enters. Calcium causes vesicles containing to fuse with the presynaptic membrane. This releases the neurotransmitter by exocytosis.

Neurotransmitter diffuses across the synaptic cleft and binds to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane. This changes ion movement and makes the receiving cell more or less likely to fire.

The chemical message must then be removed. Some neurotransmitters return to the presynaptic by ; others are broken down by enzymes. breaks down .

Step Event to explain
1 The action potential arrives at the terminal.
2 Calcium enters through channels in the terminal membrane.
3 Vesicles fuse with the presynaptic membrane and release neurotransmitter.
4 Neurotransmitter diffuses across the cleft.
5 Neurotransmitter binds postsynaptic receptors and changes the receiving cell’s .
6 Neurotransmitter is cleared; the signal can end.

On the sending side, vesicles release the message. On the receiving side, receptors bind the message and affect ion movement.

Excitatory and inhibitory effects

An excitatory signal makes an more likely. For example, Na⁺ entering the cell makes the inside less negative and moves it toward . The neuron fires only if threshold is reached.

An inhibitory signal makes an action potential less likely. In the examples here, K⁺ leaves or Cl⁻ enters. The inside becomes more negative and moves away from threshold.

Remember: excitatory input helps the neuron reach threshold; inhibitory input makes firing less likely.

Adding inputs: summation

A receives excitatory and inhibitory inputs. Summation is their combined effect. The receiving neuron fires if the combined change brings it to .

Spatial summation: inputs from different locations act together. Temporal summation: repeated inputs arrive close together in time. Both can help determine whether an occurs; they do not make it taller.

Key neurotransmitters

Know , and GABA and the examples in this table. A neurotransmitter’s effect depends on the and target tissue, so these descriptions are not universal rules.

Simplified action Secretion sites Major effects
Acetylcholine — memorize Excitatory Neuromuscular regions, , Skeletal muscle contraction / parasympathetic
Norepinephrine — memorize Excitatory CNS, PNS Wakefulness / sympathetic
Dopamine Generally excitatory CNS, PNS Voluntary movement and emotion
Serotonin Generally inhibitory CNS Sleep
GABA — memorize Inhibitory CNS Motor behaviour

At a neuromuscular junction, acetylcholine stimulates the muscle membrane and contributes to contraction. breaks down acetylcholine so that stimulation can end. Be able to explain both roles: the neurotransmitter carries the message; the enzyme helps terminate it.

Other examples include glutamate and . Dopamine, serotonin, endorphins and norepinephrine illustrate links to movement, mood, pain signalling and stress responses. These examples show why changing synaptic communication can affect many functions. Keep acetylcholine, norepinephrine and GABA as your three memorization priorities.

Receptors matter. A neurotransmitter’s effect depends on the postsynaptic receptor and the resulting membrane . Treat “excitatory” and “inhibitory” as effects at a particular , not permanent labels that explain every action of a named transmitter.

Use a normal synapse as your comparison

Start with the normal sequence: neurotransmitter is made and stored, released, bound to a , then removed. A drug can change one of these steps. You need to explain the effects, not recite the two lists.

A drug may act like a , increase its release, or slow its breakdown or . These changes can make stimulation stronger or longer-lasting.

A drug may block a receptor, reduce neurotransmitter production or storage, or speed its breakdown at the . These changes can reduce signalling through the affected pathway.

Check the kind of synapse. Blocking an excitatory receptor and blocking an inhibitory receptor can have different effects.

Lesson vocabulary

PNS · CNS · somatic nervous system · autonomic nervous system · voluntary control · sympathetic division · parasympathetic division · autonomic balance · opposing effects · effector · response · homeostasis · acetylcholine · norepinephrine · epinephrine · hormone · evidence
Select an underlined term for its definition. Your vocabulary writing is saved in Process Collection.

The PNS links the CNS with the rest of the body

The connects the brain and spinal cord with sensory organs, muscles, glands and internal organs. Sensory pathways carry information toward the ; motor pathways carry instructions away.

There are 12 pairs of cranial nerves associated with the brain and 31 pairs of spinal nerves associated with the spinal cord. You do not need to memorize the individual spinal regions here.

Somatic and autonomic systems

The includes somatic and autonomic systems. The somatic system carries sensory information and controls skeletal muscles. It includes , such as moving your hand, and skeletal-muscle reflexes.

The autonomic system controls involuntary activity in smooth muscle, heart muscle and glands. Changes in heart rate and digestion help maintain without a conscious decision.

Motor output is not always voluntary. It can also carry instructions to an that produces an involuntary .

Sympathetic: preparing for action

The produces the fight-or-flight . Pupils and air passages dilate; heart rate and blood pressure rise. Digestion and bladder emptying slow. The liver releases glucose, and adrenal secretion increases.

These changes prepare the body for action. Notice that heart activity increases while digestion decreases: not every organ speeds up.

Sympathetic nerve pathways use and . The adrenal glands can also release and norepinephrine into the blood as a signal. A blood-borne hormone is different from an impulse along an .

Parasympathetic: rest and digest

The supports rest and digest. Pupils constrict, heart rate and blood pressure fall, and digestion and urination increase. is the key in these pathways.

The often have on the same organ. Together, they adjust body functions as conditions change.

Apply it: what does a polygraph measure?

A polygraph records changes such as heart rate, blood pressure, breathing and sweating. These can reflect sympathetic activity, but they do not directly show whether someone is lying.

check: a racing heart can have several causes. The measurement alone cannot explain why it increased.

Lesson vocabulary

Select an underlined term for its definition. Your vocabulary writing is saved in Process Collection.

What the CNS does

The is the brain and spinal cord. It processes information and directs responses. Damage can affect movement, sensation, behaviour or , depending on the area involved.

Grey matter contains many cell bodies, dendrites and unmyelinated parts of axons. White matter contains many myelinated axons grouped into tracts.

In the cerebrum, grey matter forms the outer cortex, with white matter deeper inside. In a spinal cord cross-section, grey matter forms the central butterfly shape and white matter surrounds it.

The spinal cord is a communication link and a reflex centre

The spinal cord links the brain with the . Sensory information travels toward the brain; motor information travels toward effectors. The spinal cord also processes responses.

Vertebrae, meninges and cerebrospinal fluid protect the spinal cord. A vertebra is a bone; the spinal cord is the nervous tissue inside the protected canal.

An injury higher in the spinal cord can interrupt communication with more body regions below it. Explain this connection; you do not need to memorize each spinal segment.

Protecting the brain and spinal cord

The skull protects the brain. Three membrane layers, the meninges, surround the . Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) cushions the brain and spinal cord and acts as a transport medium.

The layers are dura mater, arachnoid and pia mater. CSF occupies the space between the arachnoid and pia mater and spaces within the brain. Use the diagram to locate the bone, membranes, fluid and nervous tissue.

The blood-brain barrier

The blood-brain barrier is formed by tightly joined cells in brain capillary walls. It limits what passes from the blood into tissue while allowing needed substances to reach the brain.

Different jobs: CSF cushions nervous tissue; the blood-brain barrier controls the passage of substances from blood.

Brain structures and reasoning terms

cerebrum · cerebral cortex · corpus callosum · frontal lobe · parietal lobe · temporal lobe · occipital lobe · thalamus · hypothalamus · pituitary · cerebellum · medulla oblongata · pons · midbrain · claim · evidence
Select an underlined term for its definition. Your vocabulary writing is saved in Process Collection.

Three broad regions of the brain

The brain controls conscious activities and many involuntary functions. Study its three broad regions: forebrain, midbrain and hindbrain.

Brain regions work together. For a coordinated movement, the nervous system receives sensory information, sends a motor command and adjusts the movement.

Region Structures General roles
Forebrain Cerebrum, basal ganglia, hippocampus, amygdala, thalamus, Learning and memory, conscious thought, problem solving and voluntary actions
Midbrain Tectum and tegmentum Relaying signals between forebrain and hindbrain; visual and auditory functions and alertness
Hindbrain Pons, cerebellum, medulla Breathing, heart rate, blood pressure, sleep/wake functions and balance

Focus on the main structures below. The amygdala, hippocampus and reticular formation remain optional extension topics.

Additional brain structures · extension

Optional: the amygdala is associated with emotions, the hippocampus with learning and memory, and the reticular formation with information passing through the brainstem.

Main brain structures and their functions

The cerebellum coordinates movement, balance and fine motor control. It uses information from muscles and joints to help make movements smooth and precise.

The medulla oblongata connects with the spinal cord and helps control heart rate, blood pressure, breathing, swallowing and coughing. The pons relays information between brain regions and is involved in sleep and arousal.

The midbrain relays information between the forebrain and hindbrain. It is involved in visual and auditory functions and eye movement.

The thalamus relays information, including sensory information. Below it, the regulates body temperature, hunger, thirst, heart rate and blood pressure. Its link with the connects nervous and endocrine control.

The corpus callosum is a bundle of nerve fibres connecting the left and right cerebral hemispheres. It allows them to communicate.

The cerebrum and cerebral cortex

The cerebrum is the largest part of the brain. It has left and right cerebral hemispheres. The outer cerebral cortex is grey matter. Its folds increase the surface area that fits inside the skull.

The cerebrum is part of the forebrain. The thalamus and are also part of the forebrain.

The frontal lobe is involved in thought, decisions, memory, personality and voluntary movement.

The parietal lobe processes touch and body-position information.

The temporal lobe processes hearing and contributes to language and memory.

The occipital lobe processes vision.

Motor and sensory areas

The primary motor area is in the frontal lobe. The primary somatosensory area is in the parietal lobe. The body maps are uneven: some body parts need more detailed movement control or provide more sensory information.

Many motor pathways cross in the brainstem. Damage to the right motor cortex can therefore affect movement on the left side of the body. Apply this to the motor pathway shown, not to every nervous-system structure.

The two hemispheres work together

Some functions are more strongly associated with one hemisphere, but both hemispheres work together during complex tasks.

The corpus callosum allows this communication. Avoid labelling a person as a “left-brained” or “right-brained” learner.

Select an underlined term for its definition. Your vocabulary writing is saved in Process Collection.

How can researchers connect structure with function?

Brain injuries can provide about function. For example, Phineas Gage’s frontal-lobe injury was linked with changes in behaviour and personality. One case cannot explain every function of a brain region.

Wilder Penfield stimulated parts of the brain during surgery while patients were conscious. Their movements, sensations and reported experiences helped identify sensory and motor areas.

Dissections and photographs show brain structures and their positions. Compare the surface view with a cross-section to see structures that are hidden from the outside.

MRI and PET

MRI uses magnetic fields and radio signals to create detailed images of brain structure. These images can help identify abnormalities.

PET uses a radioactive tracer. In this example, labelled glucose shows differences in energy use that can be linked to brain activity.

Compare: MRI provides structural detail; this PET example shows differences in tracer uptake. Read the scan’s key before drawing a conclusion. Neither is a direct picture of someone’s thoughts.

Bring the chapter back together

Trace a to a : → sensory neuron → → motor neuron → . In a withdrawal , the spinal circuit can start the movement before conscious processing.

At the cell level, a resting has a membrane potential. Reaching starts an . Na⁺ enters during the rise; K⁺ leaves during the fall. speeds conduction. At a chemical , neurotransmitters carry information to the next cell.

At the system level, the CNS is the brain and spinal cord. The links them with the body. Somatic pathways control skeletal muscles; autonomic pathways regulate internal organs and glands. Sympathetic and parasympathetic pathways often have opposite effects.

Before the review, explain one complete pathway aloud: name the structures, describe what happens, and connect each step to the next.

Homeostasis

Meaning

Keeping internal conditions relatively stable as conditions change.

What it does

Receptors detect a change, a control centre processes it, and effectors make adjustments.

Common confusion

-stasis
standing or condition

Use with care: The word suggests steadiness, but living systems remain dynamic and variable.

Hearing and equilibrium pathway

Hearing and equilibrium pathway

Meaning

The linked ear structures that transmit sound vibration to cochlear hair cells and detect head movement through vestibular hair-cell systems.

What it does

Sound moves the tympanic membrane and ossicles, creates cochlear fluid and membrane movement, and bends auditory hair bundles; rotational movement bends vestibular hair bundles in semicircular canals.

Common confusion

Browser tones and classroom balance activities are not diagnostic hearing or vestibular tests.

More about this word

Word structure

equilibrium
balance

Use with care: Shape words help identify anatomy but do not explain transduction.

Related ideas

Endocrine signalling

Endocrine signalling

Meaning

Longer-distance chemical communication in which endocrine cells release hormones into body fluids and only receptor-bearing target cells produce the relevant response.

What it does

A hormone is released, transported, binds a compatible receptor, and changes target-cell activity. Solubility affects receptor location and signalling mechanism.

Common confusion

A hormone in the bloodstream does not cause the same response in every tissue; receptor and intracellular machinery determine responsiveness.

More about this word

Word structure

endo-
within
-crine
secrete or separate
target
a cell capable of responding because it has the required receptor

Use with care: Hormones may travel widely, but proximity to a gland does not make every cell a target.

Related ideas

endocrine gland · hormone · target cell · receptor

Hypothalamus-pituitary axis

Hypothalamus-pituitary axis

Meaning

A coordinated signalling pathway in which the hypothalamus and pituitary connect neural information with endocrine control of other glands or direct target tissues.

What it does

Hypothalamic releasing hormones can regulate anterior-pituitary output; posterior-pituitary pathways release hormones made by hypothalamic neurons.

Common confusion

ADH is synthesized in hypothalamic neurons and released from posterior-pituitary terminals; it is not made by posterior-pituitary gland cells.

More about this word

Word structure

below
hypothalamus

tropic
acting on another endocrine tissue

Use with care: Pituitary is a historical name, and the gland is not an independent master; hypothalamic and target-gland feedback regulate it.

Antagonistic hormones

Antagonistic hormones

Meaning

Hormones whose effects push a regulated variable in opposing directions as conditions change.

What it does

Different endocrine signals favour different target-cell processes, allowing regulation in both directions rather than one hormone simply cancelling another in the bloodstream.

Common confusion

More about this word

Word structure

ant- / anti-
against or opposing
agon
contest or struggle

Use with care: The hormones need not bind one another; their physiological effects oppose each other.

Related ideas

Thyroid and calcium feedback

Thyroid and calcium feedback

Meaning

Two related endocrine contexts: a pituitary-thyroid axis regulating thyroid hormone and parathyroid/thyroid signals contributing to blood-calcium regulation.

What it does

TSH stimulates thyroid output and thyroid hormone feeds back upstream. PTH raises blood calcium through multiple targets; calcitonin can oppose some effects but is less central in adult human regulation.

Common confusion

The parathyroid glands are distinct glands on the posterior thyroid, and PTH is not secreted by thyroid follicles.

More about this word

Word structure

TSH
thyroid-stimulating hormone
PTH
parathyroid hormone
para-
beside, describing gland location
calc-
calcium-related

Use with care: Acronym expansion names the signal; it does not state every target or effect.

Related ideas

TSH · thyroxine · PTH · calcitonin

Retrieve the idea

Use high thyroxine with low TSH to identify the feedback direction without claiming a diagnosis.

Blood-glucose regulation

Blood-glucose regulation

Meaning

Endocrine regulation that coordinates glucose storage, use, and release so blood glucose remains within a workable range.

What it does

Rising glucose supports insulin release and target-cell responses; falling glucose supports glucagon release and liver glucose output. Tissue responses differ by receptor and pathway.

Common confusion

Insulin does not make every tissue respond identically, and glucagon acts principally on the liver rather than every cell.

More about this word

Word structure

sugar or glucose-related
hyper-
above or excessive
-emia
a blood condition

Use with care: Diabetes names a group of disorders; its word history does not explain the modern biological mechanism.

Related ideas

insulin · glucagon · glycogen · hyperglycemia

Meaning

Coordinated neural, endocrine, and kidney responses that regulate water balance, sodium handling, osmotic concentration, and blood volume or pressure.

Stress response

Stress response

Meaning

Nervous and hormonal responses that prepare the body for a challenge and help it recover afterward.

What it does

Fast autonomic signalling activates adrenal-medulla epinephrine release; a slower hypothalamus-pituitary-adrenal pathway supports adrenal-cortex cortisol release.

Common confusion

Cortisol and epinephrine differ in source, timing, receptor pathways, and effects; stress is not one hormone or always harmful.

More about this word

Word structure

ACTH
adrenocorticotropic hormone
adrenal
near the kidney
cortex
outer layer
medulla
inner region

Use with care: Acronym and anatomical clues identify pathway parts but do not make every stress response identical.

Related ideas

ACTH · cortisol · epinephrine · adrenal cortex

Retrieve the idea

Contrast the fast adrenal-medulla pathway with the slower ACTH-cortisol pathway.

Meaning

Adrenocorticotropic hormone, an anterior-pituitary signal regulating adrenal-cortex activity.

What it does

It stimulates cortisol secretion within the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis.

Common confusion

It does not directly name an adrenal-medulla catecholamine.

Stress response

cortisol

Meaning

An adrenal-cortex glucocorticoid hormone affecting metabolism and stress responses.

What it does

It changes substrate availability and influences many tissues through receptor-mediated regulation.

Common confusion

Cortisol is not identical to the rapid neural alarm response.

More about this word

Word structure

Cortisol is a whole hormone name; glucocorticoid identifies a steroid class, not glucose itself.

Related ideas

Stress response · ACTH · epinephrine · adrenal cortex

Retrieve the idea

Why can cortisol responses have different timing from epinephrine responses?

Stress response

epinephrine

Meaning

A hormone from the adrenal medulla, also called adrenaline.

What it does

Adrenergic receptors mediate effects supporting acute adjustments in circulation and metabolism.

Common confusion

It is not made by the adrenal cortex.

More about this word

Word structure

Epinephrine and adrenaline are alternate names for the same molecule.

Related ideas

Stress response · ACTH · cortisol · adrenal cortex

Stress response

adrenal cortex

Meaning

The outer region of the adrenal gland that produces steroid hormones.

What it does

Its zones produce hormone classes including glucocorticoids and mineralocorticoids.

Common confusion

It is distinct from the catecholamine-producing medulla.

More about this word

Word structure

Adrenal identifies the gland; cortex means its outer region.

Related ideas

Stress response · ACTH · cortisol · epinephrine

Which adrenal region produces cortisol and aldosterone?

Stress response

adrenal medulla

Meaning

The inner region of the adrenal gland containing catecholamine-secreting cells.

What it does

Sympathetic input can trigger epinephrine and norepinephrine release.

Common confusion

It does not produce the same steroid hormones as the cortex.

More about this word

Word structure

Medulla identifies an inner region; adrenal distinguishes it from other organs' medullae.

Related ideas

Stress response · ACTH · cortisol · epinephrine

Retrieve the idea

How does its neural input connect nervous and endocrine responses?
